rule.renju.note: Official renju rules. Only Black has forbidden moves (3-3, 4-4, overline); Black wins with exactly five, White with five or more. Moves 1–3 are played near the centre (the 26 openings).
rule.standard.note: No forbidden moves. Exactly five in a row wins (six or more does not count). The usual international gomoku rule.
rule.free.note: No forbidden moves. Five or more in a row wins. The most casual rule (Black, who moves first, has a big advantage).

ol.rules: Three time controls, each with a Fischer increment added after every move: Blitz (3 min + 2 s), Rapid (10 min + 5 s) and Classical (15 min + 10 s). Renju rules (Black has forbidden moves; moves 1–3 near the centre). Running out of time or resigning loses. Players with the same time control are matched first; after 20 seconds anyone may be matched (then Rapid is played). Ratings start at 1500 for all time controls and change with every result (Elo). Takebacks, hints and the evaluation are not available during a game.
ol.desc: Play people online with renju rules. Rated games change your online rating and pair you with players of similar rating. Create a room to play a friend (unrated). Who plays first (Black) is random. Your online rating is separate from the rating of rated games against the AI.
rt.desc: The AI opponent is chosen to match your rating (starts at 1000). Usually it is close to your level, sometimes clearly stronger or weaker. Wins raise your rating, losses lower it (Elo; the first 10 games move it a lot). Renju rules, colours random, 10 minutes + 5 seconds per move. No takebacks, hints or evaluation during the game (you can review it afterwards). Running out of time or leaving the game counts as a loss. The AI ratings are estimates from games between the levels.
ls.desc: New to the game? Start with "Gomoku from zero": five in a row, blocking, and the four-three. Then "Renju rules" teaches Black's forbidden moves and "Winning techniques" covers attacks with fours and key defences (20 points per problem, 75 to pass).
course.basics.sub: For complete beginners: make five → block a four → block a three → straight four → four-three, learned by playing on the board.
course.renju.sub: In renju, the official rules, only Black has forbidden moves. Learn to spot 3-3, 4-4 and overlines, and how White wins with them.
course.tactics.sub: Attacks with fours, key defensive points and attacks with threes. Good preparation for the problems.
course.graduate: 🎉 You finished "Gomoku from zero"! Try a game against the easiest AI (Lv.1) with freestyle rules (no forbidden moves).
ls.five.title: Make five
ls.five.sub: Five in a row — across, down or diagonal — wins
ls.five.intro:
Gomoku is played on the 15×15 intersections of the board. Black and White take turns placing one stone; Black goes first.

The first to get five of their stones in a row — horizontally, vertically or diagonally — wins. First, find where one more stone makes five.
ls.five.goal: Make five in a row with one move.
ls.five.hint: Look for a line with four of your stones (maybe with one gap).
ls.five.ng: {x} does not make five. The answer was {m}.
ls.block.title: Block a four
ls.block.sub: A four — one stone from five — must be blocked
ls.block.intro:
A line that needs only one more stone to make five is called a four. When your opponent has a four, you must block that point at once or you lose.

Unless you can make five yourself, blocking a four comes first.
ls.block.hint: Look for four of the opponent's stones in a line (maybe with one gap).
ls.block.ng: {x} does not stop it. Your opponent makes five at {m}.
ls.three.title: Block a three
ls.three.intro:
Three in a row with both ends open is called a three (open three). Left alone it becomes a straight four — open at both ends — which can no longer be stopped.

Block a three at one of its ends (or in the gap). In the diagram the green circles block it; the grey dots are further options.
ls.three.hint: Find three of the opponent's stones in a line (a gap is fine) with both ends open.
ls.three.why: {m} stops the three; no straight four is possible now ({n} correct points).
ls.three.ng: {x} does not stop it. Block at {m}.
ls.sfour.title: Make a straight four
ls.sfour.sub: A four open at both ends cannot be stopped
ls.sfour.intro:
Four in a row with both ends open is a straight four. The opponent can block only one end, so you make five on the next move.

Extend your three into a straight four.
ls.sfour.goal: Make a straight four (a four open at both ends).
ls.sfour.hint: Find one of your threes with both ends open.
ls.sfour.why: {m} makes a straight four. Both ends cannot be blocked at once.
ls.sfour.ng: {x} is not a straight four. The answer is {m}.
ls.fourthree.title: Win with a four-three
ls.fourthree.sub: A four and a three at the same time
ls.fourthree.intro:
A move that makes a four and a three at the same time is a four-three. The opponent must block the four, and meanwhile the three becomes a straight four — the game is won.

The four-three is the basic way to win at gomoku.
ls.fourthree.hint: Find the point where a line that becomes a four crosses a line that becomes a three.
ls.fourthree.why: {m} is a four-three. After the four is blocked, the three becomes a straight four.
ls.fourthree.ng: {x} is not a four-three. The answer is {m}.
ls.forbid33.title: The 3-3 (double three)
ls.forbid33.sub: Black may not make two threes at once
ls.forbid33.intro:
Black, moving first, has a big advantage, so in renju — the official tournament rules — only Black has moves that are not allowed: forbidden moves.

The first is the 3-3 (double three): a move that makes two threes at once. A forbidden move loses (in this app you simply cannot play it).

A three that can never become a straight four (blocked, or needing a forbidden point) does not count as a three.
ls.forbid33.goal: Where is Black's forbidden 3-3? Tap that point.
ls.forbid33.hint: Find the point where a black stone would make a three in two lines at once.
ls.forbid33.ng: {x} is not a forbidden 3-3. The forbidden point is {m}.
ls.forbid44.title: 4-4 and overline
ls.forbid44.sub: Two fours at once, or six in a row, are forbidden
ls.forbid44.intro:
Black has two more forbidden moves.

4-4 (double four): a move that makes two fours (even two fours in one line).
Overline: six or more in a row. Black must make exactly five to win.

But a move that makes exactly five is always a win for Black, even if it also makes a forbidden shape: five comes first.
ls.forbid44.goal: Where is Black's forbidden move (4-4 or overline)? Tap it.
ls.forbid44.hint: Find a point that would give Black two fours, or six or more in a row.
ls.forbid44.ng: {x} is not a forbidden 4-4 or overline. The forbidden point is {m}.
ls.fourthreeB.title: Black wins with a four-three
ls.fourthreeB.intro:
Since 3-3 and 4-4 are forbidden for Black, Black's winning shape is the four-three (one four and one three is allowed).

The board also shows forbidden points (×). Avoid them and find Black's four-three.
ls.fourthreeB.hint: You cannot play on ×. Find a point that is not × where a four line crosses a three line.
ls.fourthreeB.why: {m} is a four-three and not forbidden.
ls.fourthreeB.ng: {x} is not Black's four-three. The answer is {m}.
ls.trap.title: White's forbidden-point attack
ls.trap.intro:
White has no forbidden moves. Better still: if the point where Black must block is forbidden, Black cannot play there and loses.

Make a white four whose blocking point is forbidden for Black (×). This way of winning exists only in renju.
ls.trap.goal: White to move. Make a four Black cannot block.
ls.trap.hint: Watch the × points (forbidden for Black). Make a four whose blocking point is an ×.
ls.trap.why: The point that blocks the four at {m} is forbidden for Black. Black cannot stop it.
ls.trap.ng: Black can block after {x}. The answer is {m}.
ls.vcf.title: Attack with fours (VCF)
ls.vcf.sub: Keep making fours, then a four-three
ls.vcf.intro:
After a four the opponent must block. Making four after four, forcing the blocks, and finishing with a four-three (or a straight four) is a VCF — victory by continuous fours.

The opponent has no free move, so the right order wins for sure. Watch that a blocking stone does not give the opponent a four.
ls.vcf.goal: Play the first move of a winning series of fours.
ls.vcf.hint: Start with a four, in an order where the blocking stones do not spoil your shape.
ls.vcf.ng: {x} does not win. The answer is {m}.
ls.defend.title: Key defensive points
ls.defend.sub: Stop the attack before it starts
ls.defend.intro:
When your opponent threatens a four-three or a series of fours, block the key point before the fours and threes appear.

Many blocks look possible, but only some work. Read your opponent's next idea and choose a point that stops every attack.
ls.defend.hint: Find the point where the opponent would make a four-three or start fours, and take it first.
ls.defend.ng: After {x} your opponent still wins. Block at {m}.
ls.vct.title: Attack with threes (VCT)
ls.vct.intro:
Not only fours but also threes are attacks: if not blocked they become straight fours. Combining threes and fours to force replies and then making a four-three is a VCT — victory by continuous threats.

A three can be blocked in several ways, so choose a move that wins against every block.
ls.vct.goal: Play the first move of a winning attack (threes allowed).
ls.vct.hint: Make a three, force a block, and choose an order where the blocking stones do not help the opponent.
ls.vct.why: Starting with {m}, threes and fours win.
ls.vct.ng: {x} does not win. The answer is {m}.

rl.title: Rules
rl.lead.basic: Black and White take turns placing one stone on an intersection. The first to make five in a row — across, down or diagonally — wins. Stones are never moved or captured.
rl.board: Play on the 15×15 intersections. Black moves first. Numbering the stones in order gives the game record (the a–o and 1–15 along the edges are the coordinates).
rl.five.h: To win: five in a row
rl.five: Make five of your stones in a row, horizontally, vertically or diagonally.
rl.rules3: Freestyle: five or more wins. Standard: exactly five wins (six or more does not). Renju: Black has forbidden moves; Black wins with exactly five, White with five or more. The six black stones shown win in freestyle, but not in standard or renju.
rl.draw: If the board fills up without five in a row, the game is a draw (this almost never happens).
rl.lead.renju: To keep Black's first-move advantage in check, renju gives only Black some forbidden moves. A forbidden move loses. In this app you cannot play them, and they are marked ×. White has no forbidden moves.
rl.f33: A move that makes two threes at once. A black stone on × would make two threes (vertical and horizontal), so it is forbidden.
rl.f44: A move that makes two fours at once. Two fours in a single line (the middle point of ●·●●●·●) are also a 4-4.
rl.fol: Six or more in a row. Black must make exactly five to win; an overline is forbidden.
rl.f43: One four plus one three made at the same time is not forbidden — it is Black's basic way to win.
rl.prio: A move that makes exactly five is never forbidden, even if it also forms a 4-4 or 3-3: Black wins.
rl.white: White may play 3-3, 4-4 and overlines (six or more also wins). If the point where Black must block is forbidden, Black cannot play there and White wins.
rl.lead.terms: The shapes that decide games. Green circles mark "play here and…" points; grey dots are other places to block.
rl.four: One more stone makes five. It is a four even if one end is blocked. The opponent must block that point.
rl.sfour: A four that makes five at either end. The opponent cannot block both, so a straight four wins.
rl.three: Three in a row that becomes a straight four with one more stone. Block it right at an end (green) or one point further out (grey).
rl.split: A three with one gap. Filling the gap (green) makes a straight four, so it is also a three. Block it in the gap or at an end.
rl.lead.open: In renju the first three moves are played near the centre of the board. There are 26 possible shapes of the first three moves, called the 26 openings.
rl.open: Move 1 (Black) on the centre point (h8), move 2 (White) next to it, move 3 (Black) within two lines of the centre (grey dots). The renju rules in this app use this restriction.
rl.direct: The second move is orthogonally next to the centre. Depending on the third move there are 13 openings (Kagetsu, Kansei…).
rl.indirect: The second move is diagonally next to the centre. These also give 13 openings (Hogetsu, Chosei…).
rl.pro: Many openings are known forced wins for Black, so tournaments add opening rules (choosing openings alternately, offering two fifth moves, RIF's Taraguchi rule…). For casual play this app lets Black choose the first three moves freely. Learn the 26 openings in the "Openings" tab.

ru.place.b: Black and White take turns placing one stone on an intersection where the lines cross. Black goes first. Stones never move and are never captured.
ru.place.task: Place a black stone on any intersection (twice)

ru.five.b: The first player to line up five of their stones — across, down or diagonally — wins.

ru.five.ok: Five in a row! Black wins.

ru.block.b: A line that needs just one more stone to become five is a four. When the opponent has a four, you must block it at once or you lose.

ru.three.b: Three in a row with both ends open is a three. Extend it into a four open at both ends (a straight four) and the opponent cannot block both ends — you win.

ru.three.ok: Straight four! Whichever end White blocks, Black makes five.

ru.ol.b: In Freestyle, five or more in a row wins. In Standard, only exactly five wins — six or more (an overline) does not.

ru.f33.b: In Renju, so that Black (who moves first) is not too strong, only Black has forbidden moves. Making two threes with one stone — a 3-3 (double three) — is forbidden.

ru.f33.ok: Correct! A black stone there makes two threes, so it is forbidden (3-3).
ru.f33.ng: That is not forbidden. Look for the point that makes two threes at once.
ru.f44.b: Making two fours with one stone (4-4) and making six or more (overline) are also forbidden for Black — in Renju Black wins only with exactly five. White has no forbidden moves.
ru.f43.b: Making one four and one three at the same time — a 4-3 — is not forbidden. It is Black’s basic way to win.
ru.f43.task: Black to move. Make a 4-3 to win
ru.f43.ok: 4-3! Even after White blocks the four, the three becomes a straight four and Black wins.
ru.f43.ng: That is not a 4-3. Find the point that makes a four and a three at once.
ru.open.b: In Renju the first three moves are played near the centre: move 1 on the centre point, move 2 right next to it, move 3 within two lines of the centre.

btn.rules.title: Learn the rules
op.d.kansei: Centre, white and black stand in one vertical line. Black caps the white stone and builds from above.
op.d.keigetsu: Placed diagonally above white, touching it. A typical winning opening where black attacks quickly.
op.d.sosei: Placed far from the centre on the diagonal. The black stones are loosely connected; white is slightly better.
op.d.kagetsu: Touches both the centre and white diagonally. One of black's strongest openings and very common in play.
op.d.zangetsu: In white's row, one point apart. Black is better and white has to defend carefully.
op.d.ugetsu: Right next to the centre, so the two black stones stand side by side. Known to be a black win.
op.d.kinsei: Beside the centre with one point between. Black attacks using the gap between its stones.
op.d.shogetsu: Directly below the centre: black, black and white in one column. Black is slightly better.
op.d.kyugetsu: Diagonally below the centre. Being a little away from white, black's edge is small.
op.d.shingetsu: A wide knight's move from the centre (lower right). Considered good for black.
op.d.zuisei: Below the centre with one point between. Far from white; black is only slightly better.
op.d.sangetsu: A tall knight's move from the centre (downwards). Considered good for black.
op.d.yusei: As far from white as possible, diagonally below. The black stones do little; a white win.
op.d.chosei: Centre, white and black stand in one diagonal line beyond white. White is slightly better.
op.d.kyogetsu: Right beside white, attacking in contact. Known to be a black win.
op.d.kosei: Beside the centre with one point between, touching white diagonally. A black-win opening.
op.d.suigetsu: A wide knight's move from the centre (lower right). Considered a black win.
op.d.ryusei: Diagonally below the centre with one point between. The stones are too far apart; white is slightly better.
op.d.ungetsu: Next to the centre, directly below white. A tight cluster; considered a black win.
op.d.hogetsu: Diagonally below the centre. Together with Kagetsu the best-known black-win opening, played very often.
op.d.rangetsu: A tall knight's move from the centre (downwards). Considered a black win.
op.d.gingetsu: Directly below the centre. Away from white, but considered good for black.
op.d.myojo: Below the centre with one point between. Considered a black win.
op.d.shagetsu: White, centre and black in one diagonal line, on the side opposite white. Black is slightly better.
op.d.meigetsu: A knight's move from the centre, away from white. Considered good for black.
op.d.suisei: Diagonally opposite white with one point between. The black stones do not work together; a white win.
ri.hist: Playing “five in a row” with a Go board and stones has long been popular in Japan. Because Black, who moves first, has too big an advantage, a competitive version called Renju — with forbidden moves for Black only — was set up in Japan in the early 20th century.
ri.win: You win by being the first to get five of your stones in a row — across, down or diagonally. Depending on the rules, six or more in a row (an overline) and Black’s forbidden moves have special rules.
ri.cult: All you need is a Go board and stones, and the rules are learned in a minute, so children and adults alike play it. Renju has an international federation and world championships, and it is popular not only in Japan but also in countries such as Russia and Estonia.
